title: Greetings and introductions
objectives: I can greet people at different times of the day and say goodbye.
I can introduce myself, ask someone's name and say that I am pleased to meet them.
I can say where I am from and what nationality I am.
I can use the subject pronouns and the present tense of ser.
I can use basic politeness expressions such as por favor, obrigado, desculpa and com licença.

vocabulary.note: The most common informal greeting in Brazil, used at any time of day.
A little more formal or careful than oi. Common in writing and when speaking to a group.
Used from waking up until about noon.
Used from noon until it gets dark, around six in the evening.
Works as both a greeting and a goodbye after dark, like both good evening and good night in English.
Pronounced like 'chow'. Informal goodbye borrowed from Italian ciao.

vocabulary.en: how are you; fine, all good
vocabulary.note: Used both as the question (with rising intonation) and as the answer. A common reply is Tudo bem, e você? or Tudo ótimo.
A bit more formal than tudo bem. Answer with Bem, obrigado or Bem, obrigada.
Often shortened to just prazer. The reply can be prazer too, or o prazer é meu.

example.pt: Muito prazer, eu sou a Ana.
example.en: Nice to meet you, I am Ana.

vocabulary.note: Obrigado literally means obliged and agrees with the person speaking, not the person being thanked.
Informal apology. The more formal version is desculpe. It is also a polite way to say pardon me when you did not hear something.

vocabulary.en: excuse me (to get past or to interrupt)
vocabulary.note: Use it to pass someone, to enter a room or to politely get someone's attention. It is not an apology.
Literally how do you call yourself. The answer is Eu me chamo Ana or Meu nome é Ana.
Most country names take an article in Portuguese: o Brasil, a Argentina, os Estados Unidos.
Plural, so it takes os and the verb that follows is plural when it is the subject.

example.en: She is from the United States.

vocabulary.note: Feminine: brasileira. Nationalities are written in lower case in Portuguese.
Feminine: americana. In Brazil americano usually means from the United States.
Same form for men and women.
Feminine: mexicana.
Feminine: argentina.
Feminine: portuguesa. The accent disappears in the feminine and in the plural: portugueses.
Feminine: francesa. The accent disappears in the feminine.
Feminine: a amiga.
Use esta é when introducing a woman.
Very common in everyday speech. Que legal! means How cool!
Used with older people, strangers in formal settings and customers.

example.pt: A senhora é de São Paulo?
example.en: Are you from São Paulo, ma'am?

dialogues.title: Meeting at a party
dialogues.context: Ana and Carlos meet for the first time at a friend's party in São Paulo.

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.pt: Oi, tudo bem?
lines.en: Hi, how's it going?

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Tudo bem, e você?
lines.en: Fine, and you?

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.pt: Tudo ótimo! Eu sou o Carlos.
lines.en: Great! I am Carlos.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Muito prazer, Carlos. Eu sou a Ana.
lines.en: Nice to meet you, Carlos. I am Ana.

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.pt: Prazer, Ana! Você é brasileira?
lines.en: Nice to meet you, Ana! Are you Brazilian?

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Sou, sim. Sou de São Paulo. E você?
lines.en: Yes, I am. I am from São Paulo. And you?

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.pt: Eu sou do Rio de Janeiro.
lines.en: I am from Rio de Janeiro.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Que legal!
lines.en: How cool!

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.pt: Bom, tchau, Ana. Até amanhã!
lines.en: Well, bye, Ana. See you tomorrow!

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Tchau, Carlos!
lines.en: Bye, Carlos!

dialogues.title: A formal introduction
dialogues.context: Helena Souza and Paulo Lima meet at a business event in the afternoon. They use the formal o senhor and a senhora.

lines.speaker: Helena
lines.pt: Boa tarde. Com licença, o senhor é o senhor Lima?
lines.en: Good afternoon. Excuse me, are you Mr. Lima?

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: Sou, sim. Boa tarde! Muito prazer.
lines.en: Yes, I am. Good afternoon! Nice to meet you.

lines.speaker: Helena
lines.pt: O prazer é meu. Eu sou a Helena Souza.
lines.en: The pleasure is mine. I am Helena Souza.

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: Como vai, senhora Souza?
lines.en: How are you, Mrs. Souza?

lines.speaker: Helena
lines.pt: Bem, obrigada. E o senhor?
lines.en: Fine, thank you. And you, sir?

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: Bem, obrigado. A senhora é de Curitiba?
lines.en: Fine, thank you. Are you from Curitiba, ma'am?

lines.speaker: Helena
lines.pt: Sou, sim. E o senhor, é de onde?
lines.en: Yes, I am. And you, where are you from?

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: Eu sou de Salvador. Por favor, senhora Souza.
lines.en: I am from Salvador. After you, Mrs. Souza.

lines.speaker: Helena
lines.pt: Obrigada.
lines.en: Thank you.

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: De nada.
lines.en: You're welcome.

dialogues.title: Three friends at a language school
dialogues.context: Lucas introduces his friend Diego to Emma, a new student, before class.

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.pt: Oi, Emma! Este é o Diego. Ele é meu amigo.
lines.en: Hi, Emma! This is Diego. He is my friend.

lines.speaker: Emma
lines.pt: Oi, Diego! Muito prazer. Eu sou a Emma.
lines.en: Hi, Diego! Nice to meet you. I am Emma.

lines.speaker: Diego
lines.pt: Prazer, Emma! Você é americana?
lines.en: Nice to meet you, Emma! Are you American?

lines.speaker: Emma
lines.pt: Sou, sim. Sou dos Estados Unidos. E você?
lines.en: Yes, I am. I am from the United States. And you?

lines.speaker: Diego
lines.pt: Eu sou argentino, de Buenos Aires.
lines.en: I am Argentinian, from Buenos Aires.

lines.speaker: Emma
lines.pt: E o Lucas também é argentino?
lines.en: And is Lucas Argentinian too?

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.pt: Não, eu sou brasileiro, de Belo Horizonte.
lines.en: No, I am Brazilian, from Belo Horizonte.

lines.speaker: Diego
lines.pt: Nós somos amigos!
lines.en: We are friends!

lines.speaker: Emma
lines.pt: Que legal! Até amanhã, Diego. Até amanhã, Lucas.
lines.en: How cool! See you tomorrow, Diego. See you tomorrow, Lucas.

lines.speaker: Lucas
lines.pt: Tchau, Emma!
lines.en: Bye, Emma!

grammar.title: Subject pronouns
grammar.explanation:
Subject pronouns say who does the action. Brazilian Portuguese has a smaller everyday set than textbooks often show. For one person you say eu (I), você (you), ele (he) and ela (she). For more than one you say nós (we), vocês (you, plural), eles (they, masculine or mixed group) and elas (they, all female).

In everyday speech a gente (literally the people) replaces nós for we. It looks plural but takes the same verb form as você, ele and ela: a gente é brasileiro. Nós is still correct and is more common in writing.

Você is the normal word for you in most of Brazil, with friends, strangers and colleagues alike. The formal forms are o senhor (to a man) and a senhora (to a woman). In some regions, such as the far south, parts of the northeast and some areas of Rio, you will also hear tu for a close friend, but você is understood everywhere and is the safest choice. The forms tu and vós that you may see in European Portuguese grammar tables are not needed at this stage.

Portuguese often drops the subject pronoun because the verb ending shows who is speaking. Eu sou brasileiro and Sou brasileiro are both normal. Keep the pronoun when you want emphasis or when it would be unclear.

examples.pt: A gente é de São Paulo.

grammar.title: The verb ser in the present
grammar.explanation:
Ser is one of the two Portuguese verbs for to be. In this unit you use it to say who someone is, where they are from and their nationality. It is irregular, so learn the forms as a block. Eu sou, você é, ele é, ela é, nós somos, a gente é, vocês são, eles são, elas são.

Notice that você, ele, ela and a gente all share the form é, and vocês, eles and elas all share são. That means you only have to remember four different forms: sou, é, somos and são.

To ask a question you usually keep the same word order as a statement and raise your voice at the end: Você é brasileiro? There is no word like do or does. To answer yes you can repeat the verb instead of saying sim: Você é brasileira? Sou. Adding sim is also fine and very common: Sou, sim.

The pronunciation matters. Sou sounds like 'so' with a quick w glide at the end. The forms é and são are short and clear: é is like the e in 'bed' and são ends with a nasal sound that you will study in the sounds unit.

grammar.title: Saying where you are from and your nationality
grammar.explanation:
To say where you are from, use ser followed by de: Eu sou de São Paulo. With a city name, de stays as it is. Country names usually take an article, and de joins with it: de + o = do, de + a = da, de + os = dos. So you say Eu sou do Brasil, Ela é da Argentina, Eles são dos Estados Unidos. Portugal is an exception with no article: Ele é de Portugal. A few cities also take an article, such as Rio de Janeiro: Eu sou do Rio.

To ask the question, use De onde você é? or Você é de onde? Both are natural. To ask about the person's nationality you can just ask Você é brasileiro?

Nationalities are adjectives and agree with the person. Most end in -o for men and change to -a for women: brasileiro, brasileira. Words ending in -ense or -ista do not change: canadense. Words ending in a consonant such as português and francês add -a for the feminine and lose their written accent: portuguesa, francesa. Nationalities are not capitalized in Portuguese.

Note that americano in Brazil almost always means from the United States, even though Brazilians are also from the Americas.

examples.en: They are from the United States.

grammar.title: Greeting and politeness formulas
grammar.explanation:
Greetings depend on the time of day: bom dia until about noon, boa tarde in the afternoon and boa noite after dark. Boa noite also means good night when you leave. Oi works at any time and is the usual informal hello. Tchau and até logo are goodbyes, and até amanhã means see you tomorrow.

Tudo bem? is the most common way to ask how someone is. It works like how's it going in English, and the answer is also Tudo bem, usually followed by e você? Como vai? is slightly more formal. You can reply Bem, obrigado if you are a man and Bem, obrigada if you are a woman. The word obrigado agrees with the person who is speaking.

When you meet someone, say Muito prazer or just Prazer. To introduce yourself, say Eu sou o Carlos or Meu nome é Carlos. Brazilians often put the article before a first name in casual speech: a Ana, o Carlos. To ask someone's name, say Como você se chama?

For manners: por favor means please, de nada means you're welcome, com licença is used to pass someone or interrupt politely, and desculpa is for apologies. Do not use desculpa to get past someone, because com licença is the correct phrase for that.

examples.pt: Muito prazer, eu me chamo Ana.
examples.en: Nice to meet you, my name is Ana.

culture.title: How Brazilians greet each other
culture.text:
Brazilians are warm and physical greeters. Friends and family greet with a hug, and women, and men and women together, often exchange kisses on the cheek. One kiss is common in São Paulo, two in Rio de Janeiro and in many other places, and in parts of Minas Gerais you may get three. Men shake hands or hug. In business settings a handshake is standard the first time you meet.

First names are used almost everywhere, even with your boss or your doctor. Titles still appear with older people and in formal situations: senhor, senhora, and dona before a woman's first name, as in Dona Maria. In some regions you will also hear seu before a man's first name, as in seu João.

Tudo bem? works as a greeting even when you are not really asking a question. People often answer Tudo! or Tudo bem, e você? and keep walking. Arriving somewhere, it is polite to greet everyone in the room with a general bom dia or boa tarde before you say anything else.

Finally, Brazilian Portuguese is spoken differently from the Portuguese of Portugal, and you will often hear both accents on the internet. In this course you learn Brazilian forms such as você and a gente.

exercises.explanation: Boa tarde is used from noon until it gets dark.

exercises.prompt: Which pronoun is the everyday spoken word for 'we' and takes the same verb form as você?
exercises.explanation: A gente means we but uses the third person singular verb: a gente é.

exercises.prompt: Someone says 'Tudo bem?' to you. What is a normal reply?
exercises.explanation: Tudo bem is both the question and the usual answer.

exercises.prompt: A woman wants to say 'thank you'. Which word does she use?
exercises.explanation: Obrigado and obrigada agree with the person speaking.

exercises.prompt: You need to get past someone on a crowded bus. What do you say?
exercises.explanation: Com licença is used to pass someone. Desculpa is an apology.
Eles is they and são is the plural form of ser.

exercises.prompt: Which expression is the formal word for 'you' when speaking to a man?
exercises.explanation: O senhor is formal you for a man and a senhora is formal you for a woman.
Sou is the eu form of ser.
Somos is the nós form of ser.
Ela, ele and você all use é.
Vocês, eles and elas use são.
Muito prazer is the standard phrase when meeting someone.
De + a becomes da before a feminine country name.
The subject pronoun can be dropped, and the article before the name is optional.

exercises.prompt_en: We are Brazilian. (a group of men)
exercises.explanation: A gente is singular in form, so the adjective stays singular.

exercises.audio_pt: Muito prazer, eu sou a Ana.
exercises.hint_en: Nice to meet you, I am Ana.
